title: Debug and extend a maze class
label: single
statement: You are handed a maze class with bugs. Fix it, then extend it: validate that it is well formed, find the shortest path, and generate mazes that always have a path.
provenance: Reported once for LinkedIn's AI-enabled round. Reported wording: A buggy maze class to debug and build out with the built-in assistant. Follow-ups, verbatim: "How would you make sure the maze is well formed, including the outer wall?" · "Given a start and end position, how would you generate the maze so there is always a path?" · "Why did you choose this AI-generated approach over the other options?" · "How would you test each change?" · "If this went to production, what would you change?"

stages.title: Debug the existing class
stages.say: This Maze class has bugs — ShortestPath is sometimes wrong and sometimes crashes. Find and fix them. Read it before you prompt.
stages.require: Fix `ShortestPath()` so it returns the fewest steps (or -1), never indexes outside the grid, and never enqueues a cell twice. Also reject an empty or ragged grid in the constructor with `ArgumentException`.

stages.say: How would you make sure the maze is well formed, including the outer wall?

stages.title: Always a path
stages.say: Given a start and an end position, how would you generate the maze so that there is always a path?

testNames: 200 generated mazes: well formed and solvable

flaw.ctx: The assistant produced this. Later a user reported: "Distance is right, but the queue holds about twice as many entries as there are cells."
flaw.answer: Cells are marked visited on **dequeue**, so a cell can be enqueued once per neighbour before it is processed. **7,081 enqueues for 3,600 cells** on a 60×60 grid; on a word graph with ~25 neighbours per node the factor is ~25×.

qa.a: Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md: You are handed a maze class with bugs. Fix it, then extend it: validate that it is well formed, find the shortest path, and generate mazes that always have a path.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Parse a grid of `#`, `.`, `S`, `E`
- `IsWellFormed`: closed outer wall except S/E openings; S ≠ E
- `ShortestPath`: BFS step count or −1
- `Generate(rows, cols, seed)` with a guaranteed path

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Debug-first rounds score reading. Read the class, state its invariants, write the failing test, then fix. For generation: carving a **spanning tree** over the cells (randomised DFS) connects every open cell, so S and E are connected by construction — no need to generate-and-check.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: Constructor validates shape (non-empty, rectangular). BFS marks distance on enqueue. Generator is iterative so a large maze cannot overflow the stack.

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- BFS: mark on enqueue; bounds check before indexing.
- Generate: odd dimensions; start at (1,1); repeatedly carve to a random unvisited cell two steps away, knocking out the wall between.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Type | Why |
|---|---|
| bool[,] | Walls; O(1) lookup |
| int[,] dist (−1 = unseen) | Visited and distance in one array |
| Queue<(int,int)> | BFS frontier |
| Stack<(int,int)> | Iterative DFS carving |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
- BFS: mark on enqueue; bounds check before indexing.
- Generate: odd dimensions; start at (1,1); repeatedly carve to a random unvisited cell two steps away, knocking out the wall between.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md: BFS O(rows × cols). Generation O(rows × cols).

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
- Hand-made 5×7 maze: well formed, path 8.
- A hole in the outer wall is detected.
- A walled-off E returns −1.
- 200 generated mazes (seeds 0–199, 21×31): every one well formed and solvable.

learn.title: 10 · Tests
learn.md:
**S1 — Debug the existing class**

- shortest path
- no path
- S on the edge with an open neighbour off-grid
- open 60x60 grid
- ragged grid rejected
- empty grid rejected

**S2 — Is it well formed?**

- well formed
- hole in the outer wall detected
- too small

**S3 — Always a path**

- 200 generated mazes: well formed and solvable
- same seed, same maze
- even dimensions rejected

learn.title: 11 · AI usage strategy
learn.md:
- Start with: "Summarise this class, its invariants, and any method inconsistent with the others. Quote line numbers."
- Do not ask it to "fix the bugs" — ask for hypotheses, verify, then fix.
- Ask for two generation algorithms and their trade-offs, then choose.

**Prompts for this question:**

- *Check my design — no code* — "I believe BFS that marks a cell visited when it is enqueued and checks bounds before indexing, and a randomised DFS that carves a spanning tree so every open cell — including S and E — is connected by construction. Review my reasoning without giving me the implementation. What would break it?"
- *Review, do not rewrite* — "Review my implementation for correctness and edge cases. Do not rewrite the code. List problems most severe first, each with the input that triggers it."
- *Race conditions* — "Now review this implementation for race conditions if multiple threads call ShortestPath queries on a shared maze concurrently. For each race, give the interleaving that breaks it. Then name the smallest synchronization boundary that preserves correctness. Do not write code yet."
- *Tests that expose bugs* — "Suggest tests that could expose bugs in my implementation: boundaries, duplicates, empty and invalid input, and concurrency where it applies. For each, say why the expected value is correct."
- *Complexity check* — "What is the time and space complexity of each public method as written? Do not claim a bound unless every step achieves it."
- *Requirement change* — "The requirement changed: Add bool IsWellFormed(): at least 3×3; the whole border is wall except that S and E may sit on it; S and E are distinct open cells. List which members need to change and which do not, before writing any code."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Recursive DFS generator: stack overflow on a large maze.
- BFS marking visited on dequeue (D3).
- Bounds check after the array access.
- Even dimensions with the step-2 carving: the last row/column is unreachable.

**Verification exercise:** Bug — Cells are marked visited on **dequeue**, so a cell can be enqueued once per neighbour before it is processed. **7,081 enqueues for 3,600 cells** on a 60×60 grid; on a word graph with ~25 neighbours per node the factor is ~25×.

learn.title: 13 · Concurrency considerations
learn.md:
Not inherently concurrent. If asked: the maze is immutable after construction, so concurrent path queries need no locks — say that, it is the right answer.

**Level 3 — Concurrency**

- *Many path queries at once.* — Immutable after construction → no locks

learn.title: 14 · Scalability considerations
learn.md:
**Level 4 — Scale**

- *A 10,000 × 10,000 maze.* — Bit-packed walls; bidirectional BFS

learn.title: 15 · Production considerations
learn.md:
- Reject huge dimensions before allocating.
- Seeded generation so a reported maze can be reproduced.

**Level 5 — Productionisation**

- *A user reports a broken maze.* — Seeded generation reproduces it

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
- *Fix the bugs.* — Failing test first, then the fix, keep the test.
- *Well formed including the outer wall.* — Border all wall except openings; S/E distinct and open.
- *Always a path.* — Spanning-tree carving, or union-find (Kruskal) — say why both guarantee connectivity.
- *Why did you choose the AI's approach?* — Have a reason: "It suggested DFS backtracking and Kruskal. DFS is simpler to verify and iterative avoids stack depth; Kruskal gives less biased mazes. Simplicity won here."
- *How would you test each change?* — One test per change, plus the property test over many seeds.
- *Production?* — Validate input size, bound generation time, make seeds reproducible for support tickets.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *Empty, ragged, no S or E, S equals E?* — Constructor validation; IsWellFormed rules

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *BFS cost? Generation cost?* — O(cells) each
- *Very large maze?* — Iterative generation; memory O(cells)

aiGuide.intro: Debug-and-extend: you are handed a class with bugs. **Reproduce each report with a test before asking anything** — the AI is a second reader here, not an author.
plan: Read the class. Reproduce each user report with a tiny failing input
AI as second reader: explain the cause of each failing input — no rewrite
Fix by hand, run, count enqueues
IsWellFormed: you define it; AI implements
Generate: AI writes randomised DFS; 200 seeds must be solvable
Follow-ups: A*, weighted cells, huge grids

stages.name: Debug the existing class
stages.yours: Read the class first. Turn each report into a failing input: `"S.E"` (start on the edge), an empty grid, a ragged grid, an open 60×60 grid. Run them **before** prompting.
stages.ai: **AI reviews** — with your failing inputs. Ask for causes and minimal diffs, never a rewrite.
bad: Fix the bugs in this code.
A rewrite: new structure, two bugs fixed, a third introduced — and you cannot see what changed.
No failing inputs, so it guesses which bugs matter
A rewrite destroys the diff you need to review
You learn nothing you can say out loud
good: Here are failing inputs for the Maze class below: "S.E" throws IndexOutOfRangeException; an empty or ragged grid crashes later instead of in the constructor; a 60×60 open grid enqueues far more cells than it has. For each, explain the cause in one sentence, pointing at the line. Do not rewrite the class — minimal diffs only. Keep my class structure; no new public members.
stages.reply: Typical reply finds **bounds checked after indexing** and the missing input validation, and often **misses** visited-on-dequeue (verified planted flaw D3) — the result is still correct, so only counting enqueues proves it.
validate: Start on the edge: neighbours off-grid are skipped before indexing
Empty and ragged grids throw ArgumentException in the constructor
Each cell enqueued at most once — mark visited on enqueue
stages.fix: Each fix is one to three lines → **by hand**, one at a time, re-running after each.
stages.say: "Bounds before indexing; visited on enqueue — the result was right before, but the queue held twice the cells."
stages.require: Fix `ShortestPath()` so it returns the fewest steps (or -1), never indexes outside the grid, and never enqueues a cell twice. Also reject an empty or ragged grid in the constructor with `ArgumentException`.
stages.say_iv: This Maze class has bugs — ShortestPath is sometimes wrong and sometimes crashes. Find and fix them. Read it before you prompt.

stages.name: Always a path
stages.yours: Define "well formed" yourself (closed outer wall except S and E, at least 3×3, S ≠ E). For generation, say why it must be connected: **randomised DFS carving builds a spanning tree**, so every open cell — S and E included — is reachable.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** Generate, then test it on 200 seeds.
bad: Random walls at some density. Some seeds have no path at all.
good: Add static Maze Generate(int rows, int cols, int seed): odd dimensions >= 5 (else ArgumentException), start all walls, carve with an iterative randomised depth-first search from (1,1) using new Random(seed), jumping two cells and opening the wall between. Put S at (1,1) and E at (rows-2, cols-2). Iterative, not recursive. Keep my existing methods unchanged; no new public members. Explain why every maze it makes has a path. Show only Generate.
The **guarantee** comes from the algorithm named
stages.reply: Typical defect: **recursive** DFS — fine at 21×31, stack overflow on a big grid. Or a non-seeded Random.
validate: 200 seeds: every maze well formed and solvable
stages.fix: Recursion → **a follow-up**: "Make the carving iterative with an explicit Stack<(int,int)>."
stages.say: "DFS carving builds a spanning tree of the cells, so a path always exists — I check 200 seeds rather than trusting one."
stages.require: Add `static Maze Generate(int rows, int cols, int seed)` for odd dimensions ≥ 5 (others throw `ArgumentException`): S at (1,1), E at (rows−2, cols−2), well formed, always solvable, deterministic for a seed.
stages.say_iv: Given a start and an end position, how would you generate the maze so that there is always a path?

none: You think and write. This is what is scored.
check: Ask it to attack your design or maths — no code.
cogen: Your design, pasted; the AI fills in mechanical code you can verify fast.
tests: Boilerplate you can check: ask for a reason per expected value.
